git: You just made a commit and nothing is staged. What does git commit --amend do?
Replaces the last commit with a new one and lets you edit its message
Adds a new empty commit on top with the same message
Reverts the last commit and keeps its changes staged
Pushes the last commit to the remote with a new message
--amend rewrites the tip commit: it creates a new commit (new hash) with the staged content and an editable message, replacing the old one.
Which command commits modifications to already tracked files without running git add first?
git commit -a -m "fix"
git commit -s -m "fix"
git commit -n -m "fix"
git commit --staged -m "fix"
-a automatically stages modified and deleted tracked files. -s adds a Signed-off-by line and -n skips hooks; neither stages anything.
app.js is tracked and modified; notes.txt is new and was never added. What does git commit -a -m "wip" include?
Only the changes to app.js
Both app.js and notes.txt
Only the new file notes.txt
Nothing, because nothing was staged
commit -a stages changes to tracked files only. Untracked files such as notes.txt still need an explicit git add.
How do teams practicing trunk-based development usually integrate their work?
Short-lived branches or small commits merged into main at least daily
Long-lived feature branches merged into main at release time
A develop branch plus separate release and hotfix branches
One permanent branch per developer, merged once per quarter
Trunk-based development keeps branches very short-lived so main is integrated continuously. A develop branch with release and hotfix branches describes Git Flow.
In the Git Flow branching model, which branch is a hotfix branch created from?
main (the production branch)
develop
the newest feature branch
the most recent release branch
Git Flow hotfixes start from the production branch (main or master) and are merged back into both main and develop.
You are on branch feature and run git rebase main. What happens?
Feature's commits are replayed on top of main, getting new commit hashes
A merge commit joining main into feature is created
Main's commits are moved onto feature with unchanged hashes
All feature commits are squashed into one commit on main
Rebase rewrites the branch: each feature commit is reapplied on the tip of main, producing new commits with new hashes and a linear history.
Why should you avoid rebasing commits that are already pushed to a shared branch others work on?
It rewrites history, so collaborators' copies diverge from the new commits
It deletes the remote branch after the rebase finishes
It permanently removes the original commit messages
It disables fast-forward merges for the whole repository
Rebased commits are new objects. Anyone who based work on the old commits now has diverging history and must reconcile it, often painfully.
A fast-forward is possible. What does git merge --no-ff feature do?
Creates a merge commit anyway
Fails with an error
Performs a fast-forward
Rebases feature onto the current branch
--no-ff forces a merge commit even when Git could simply move the branch pointer, which keeps a visible record of the feature branch.
During git merge feature, a file contains <<<<<<< HEAD, then =======, then >>>>>>> feature. What is between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======?
The version from your current branch
The version from the feature branch
The common ancestor's version
The combined result Git suggests
HEAD is the branch you are merging into, so its side comes first. The part after ======= up to >>>>>>> feature is the incoming branch's version.
You fixed the conflict markers in config.yml during a merge. How do you tell Git the conflict is resolved?
Stage the file with git add, then commit
Run git resolve config.yml
Run git merge --skip
Delete the .git/MERGE_HEAD file
Staging a file marks its conflict as resolved. Once all files are staged, git commit (or git merge --continue) completes the merge.
A merge produced many conflicts and you want to return to the state before you started it. Which command does that?
git merge --abort
git merge --undo
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git checkout --theirs .
git merge --abort restores the pre-merge state. reset --soft HEAD~1 would move the branch back one existing commit, since the merge was never committed.
What does git cherry-pick abc123 do?
Applies the changes of commit abc123 as a new commit on the current branch
Moves abc123 to the current branch and removes it from its original branch
Checks out commit abc123 in detached HEAD state
Merges the entire branch that contains abc123
Cherry-pick copies one commit's changes into a new commit on HEAD. The original commit stays where it was.
Which git cherry-pick option appends a line like (cherry picked from commit ...) to the new commit message?
-x
-n
-e
-s
-x records the source commit hash in the message. -n applies changes without committing, -e opens the editor and -s adds a Signed-off-by line.
A bad commit is already pushed to a shared main branch. Which command undoes it without rewriting history?
git revert <commit>
git reset --hard <commit>~1
git commit --amend
git rebase -i <commit>~1
git revert adds a new commit that reverses the changes, so others can pull normally. Reset, amend and interactive rebase all rewrite history.
What does git reset --soft HEAD~1 do?
Moves the branch back one commit and keeps its changes staged
Moves the branch back one commit and keeps its changes unstaged
Moves the branch back one commit and discards its changes
Adds a new commit that undoes the last commit
--soft only moves the branch pointer; index and working tree are untouched, so the changes stay staged. Unstaged is --mixed, discarded is --hard.
What mode does git reset HEAD~1 use when no mode option is given?
--mixed
--soft
--hard
--keep
The default is --mixed: the branch and index move back, but the working tree keeps the changes as unstaged modifications.
You ran git reset --hard HEAD~3 by mistake. Which command most directly shows the hash of the commit you were on before?
git reflog
git log --oneline
git stash list
git status
The reflog records every move of HEAD, including resets, so the old tip appears there. git log only shows commits reachable from the current HEAD.
Which statement about git reflog is true?
It is local to your repository and is not pushed to remotes
It is uploaded to the remote together with your commits
It records merge commits only, not resets or checkouts
It is stored inside every commit object as metadata
The reflog lives in .git/logs of your clone and expires over time. It is a local safety net, not shared history.
You cloned a repository that uses submodules and the submodule folders are empty. Which command fetches and checks them out?
git submodule update --init --recursive
git submodule add --recursive
git pull --submodules-only
git fetch --all-submodules
update --init registers the submodules from .gitmodules and checks out the recorded commits; --recursive handles nested ones. Cloning with --recurse-submodules does this upfront.
What does the parent repository record for each submodule?
A specific commit hash of the submodule repository
A full copy of the submodule's history
The submodule branch name, followed to its newest commit
A compressed snapshot of the submodule's files
The parent stores a gitlink entry pointing to one exact commit, plus the URL in .gitmodules. Updating the submodule means committing a new pointer.
github-actions: Where must workflow files be stored for GitHub Actions to detect them?
.github/workflows/
.github/actions/
.actions/workflows/
workflows/ at the repository root
GitHub only loads workflow YAML files from the .github/workflows directory of the repository.
A workflow defines three jobs with no needs keys. How do they run?
In parallel, each on its own runner
One after another in file order
One after another in alphabetical order
In parallel, all on the same runner machine
Jobs are independent and run concurrently by default. Use needs to create dependencies between them.
Job deploy must start only after jobs build and test succeed. Which key do you add to deploy?
needs: [build, test]
depends_on: [build, test]
after: [build, test]
requires: [build, test]
needs declares job dependencies; deploy waits for both and is skipped if either fails (unless you change it with an if condition).
In one job, step 1 writes out.txt into the workspace. Can step 2 of the same job read it?
Yes, steps of a job share the runner's filesystem
No, each step starts in a fresh container
Only if out.txt is uploaded as an artifact
Only if step 2 declares needs on step 1
All steps of a job run sequentially on the same runner, so files persist between them. Artifacts are needed only to pass files between jobs.
Job build produces a dist/ folder that job publish needs. What is the standard way to pass it?
Upload it with actions/upload-artifact, then download it with actions/download-artifact
Read it from ../build/dist inside the publish job
Do nothing, since all jobs share one workspace
Add needs: build, which copies the workspace over
Each job runs on a separate runner, so files must be shared through artifacts. needs only orders jobs; it does not copy files.
Which step key runs shell commands such as npm test on the runner?
run
uses
with
exec
run executes commands in a shell. uses calls an action, and with passes inputs to that action.
What is the recommended way for a step to set an output named version?
echo "version=1.2.3" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
echo "::set-output name=version::1.2.3"
echo "version=1.2.3" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
export version=1.2.3
Writing to the GITHUB_OUTPUT file sets a step output. The ::set-output command is deprecated, and GITHUB_ENV sets an environment variable instead.
Which is a key characteristic of a GitHub-hosted runner?
Each job gets a fresh virtual machine that is discarded afterwards
It keeps files from previous jobs between workflow runs
It runs on hardware inside your own data center
It must be registered manually with a registration token
GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral VMs managed by GitHub. Persistent state and manual registration describe self-hosted runners.
Why does GitHub advise against self-hosted runners on public repositories?
A pull request from a fork could run untrusted code on your machine
Self-hosted runners cannot be attached to public repositories
Self-hosted runners do not support Docker containers
Self-hosted runners cannot read repository secrets
Anyone can open a pull request on a public repo, and workflow code from it could execute on your persistent machine and compromise it.
Which runs-on value targets a self-hosted runner that has the custom label gpu?
runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu]
runs-on: self-hosted:gpu
runs-on: gpu-hosted
runs-on: ubuntu-latest-gpu
runs-on accepts a list of labels, and the job goes to a runner that has all of them. self-hosted is the default label of every self-hosted runner.
Which trigger runs a workflow only for pushes to the main branch?
on: { push: { branches: [main] } }
on: { push: { tags: [main] } }
on: { pull_request: { branches: [main] } }
on: { push: { paths: [main] } }
The branches filter limits push events to matching branch names. pull_request with branches: [main] runs for pull requests targeting main, not pushes.
A workflow is triggered by pull_request from a fork. Which is true about secrets?
Repository secrets are not passed, and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only
All repository secrets are available as usual
Secrets are available only in the first job
Secrets are passed but their values are encrypted
To protect secrets from untrusted code, fork pull requests get no repository secrets (except GITHUB_TOKEN) and the token has read-only permissions.
Which event lets you start a workflow manually with a Run workflow button in the Actions tab?
workflow_dispatch
workflow_run
repository_dispatch
workflow_call
workflow_dispatch adds a manual trigger in the UI (and the API). repository_dispatch is API-only, workflow_run follows another workflow and workflow_call is for reusable workflows.
A workflow has on: { push: { paths: ['docs/**'] } }. When does it run?
Only when a push changes at least one file under docs/
On every push, but it checks out only the docs/ folder
On every push except those that change docs/
Only on pushes to branches whose names start with docs
The paths filter runs the workflow when any changed file matches the pattern. paths-ignore is the opposite filter.
How do you reference a repository secret named API_KEY in a workflow file?
${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
${{ env.API_KEY }}
${{ vars.API_KEY }}
${{ github.API_KEY }}
Secrets are accessed through the secrets context. vars is the context for non-secret configuration variables.
A step accidentally prints the exact value of a registered secret to the log. What appears in the log?
The value is replaced with ***
The value in plain text
Nothing, the job fails at once
A hash of the secret value
GitHub masks registered secret values in logs. Masking can miss transformed values (for example base64), so avoid printing secrets at all.
MODE is set to a under the workflow-level env and to b under a step's env. Which value does that step see?
b
a
An empty string
The job fails due to the conflict
More specific scopes win: step env overrides job env, which overrides workflow env.
What is GITHUB_TOKEN in a workflow run?
A token GitHub creates automatically for the run, scoped to the repository
A personal access token you must create and store first
A permanent token shared by all repositories you own
The repository's SSH deploy key, exposed as a variable
GitHub generates GITHUB_TOKEN for each job, limited to the repository and to the permissions you grant, and it expires when the job ends.
Which three kinds of custom actions can you create for GitHub Actions?
JavaScript, Docker container and composite
JavaScript, Python and Bash
Docker, Kubernetes and Helm
Composite, matrix and reusable
Custom actions are JavaScript actions, Docker container actions or composite actions. Reusable workflows and matrices are workflow features, not action types.
Which file defines a custom action's inputs, outputs and how it runs?
action.yml
workflow.yml
package.json
Dockerfile
Every action has a metadata file named action.yml (or action.yaml) with name, inputs, outputs and the runs section.
gitlab-ci: By default, where does GitLab look for a project's pipeline configuration?
.gitlab-ci.yml in the repository root
.gitlab/ci.yml in the repository root
gitlab-ci.yaml inside a .ci folder
pipeline.yml inside a .gitlab folder
GitLab reads .gitlab-ci.yml from the root by default. The path can be changed in the project's CI/CD settings, but that is the default.
If .gitlab-ci.yml has no stages keyword, which stages are available?
.pre, build, test, deploy and .post
build, test and deploy only
test only
prepare, build, release and cleanup
Without a stages list GitLab uses build, test and deploy, plus the special .pre and .post stages that run first and last.
A job has no stage keyword. Which stage does it run in?
test
build
.pre
the first stage in the stages list
Jobs without an explicit stage are assigned to the test stage.
Without needs, how do jobs in the same stage and the next stage run?
Same-stage jobs run in parallel; the next stage starts after all succeed
Same-stage jobs run one by one in file order
Same-stage jobs run in parallel; the next starts once any succeeds
Each stage may contain only one job, run in order
Stages run in sequence, and jobs within a stage run concurrently (given free runners). A failed job stops later stages unless it has allow_failure.
Which keyword lets a job start as soon as specific jobs finish, without waiting for the whole previous stage?
needs
dependencies
depends_on
after_script
needs builds a directed acyclic graph so jobs can skip stage ordering. dependencies only controls which artifacts are downloaded.
Which keyword must every regular (non-trigger) GitLab CI job define?
script
image
stage
tags
script holds the commands the runner executes and is required. image, stage and tags are optional and have defaults.
What does it mean when a job name starts with a dot, such as .node-template?
It is a hidden job that does not run and can be reused with extends
It runs in the .pre stage before every other job
It runs only for pipelines on the default branch
It runs only after a user starts it manually
Jobs whose names start with a dot are ignored by the pipeline. They are commonly used as templates through extends or YAML anchors.
Which rule makes a job run only in merge request pipelines?
- if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
- if: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST == "true"
- if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "merge_request"
- if: $CI_JOB_SOURCE == "merge_request"
CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE is merge_request_event for merge request pipelines. The other variables shown do not exist with those values.
What does when: manual do on a job?
The job waits until a user starts it from the UI or API
The job runs only when a previous job has failed
The job runs only on scheduled pipelines
The job is skipped and cannot be started later
Manual jobs appear with a play button and run only when someone triggers them, a common pattern for production deploys.
What does artifacts: paths: [dist/] on a build job do?
Uploads dist/ after the job so later jobs and users can download it
Caches dist/ between pipelines to speed up installs
Commits dist/ back to the repository after the job
Keeps dist/ only for the steps of the same job
Artifacts are job outputs stored by GitLab. Jobs in later stages download them by default, and users can download them from the UI.
A deploy-stage job sets dependencies: [build-web]. What effect does this have?
It downloads artifacts only from build-web, not from other earlier jobs
It waits for build-web even when both are in the same stage
It reruns build-web right before the deploy job starts
It lets the deploy job pass even if build-web fails
dependencies limits which earlier jobs' artifacts are fetched. An empty list, dependencies: [], downloads none.
A test job writes reports you need especially when tests fail. Which setting uploads its artifacts even on failure?
artifacts: when: always
artifacts: on: failure
artifacts: allow_failure: true
artifacts: expire_in: never
artifacts:when accepts on_success (default), on_failure and always. allow_failure is a job keyword and expire_in only sets retention.
Which statement correctly contrasts cache and artifacts in GitLab CI?
Cache reuses dependencies to speed up jobs; artifacts pass outputs to later stages
Artifacts reuse dependencies to speed jobs; cache passes outputs to later stages
Cache is guaranteed to exist; artifacts are best-effort and may be missing
Both behave the same way; only the keyword name differs
Cache is a best-effort speedup (for example node_modules) and may be missing. Artifacts are reliable job outputs for later jobs and downloads.
What does cache: key: files: [package-lock.json] achieve?
A new cache key is used whenever package-lock.json changes
Only package-lock.json is stored in the cache
The job is skipped if package-lock.json did not change
package-lock.json is uploaded as a job artifact
The key is computed from the listed files' content, so dependencies are reinstalled and recached only when the lock file changes.
A test job should only read the shared node_modules cache and never upload it. Which cache setting fits?
policy: pull
policy: push
policy: pull-push
policy: readonly
pull downloads the cache but skips uploading it at the end, saving time. pull-push is the default, and push only uploads.
Which job keyword selects runners that have a specific label, such as docker-arm?
tags
runner
labels
runs-on
tags matches jobs to runners registered with the same tags. runs-on is the GitHub Actions equivalent.
Which kind of GitLab runner is available to every project in a GitLab instance?
Instance runner
Group runner
Project runner
Protected runner
Instance runners (formerly called shared runners) serve all projects. Group runners serve one group's projects, project runners a single project.
Which GitLab Runner executor runs each job in a fresh container created from the job's image?
docker
shell
ssh
parallels
The docker executor starts a container from the image keyword for each job. The shell executor runs commands directly on the runner host.
Which predefined variable holds the short commit SHA in a GitLab CI job?
$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
$CI_SHORT_SHA
$GITLAB_COMMIT_SHA
$CI_SHA_SHORT
CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA is the first eight characters of CI_COMMIT_SHA, often used for image tags.
What does marking a CI/CD variable as Protected do?
It is exposed only to pipelines on protected branches or tags
It is hidden from job logs by replacing it with stars
It cannot be overridden by values in .gitlab-ci.yml
It is readable only by users with the Owner role
Protected limits where a variable is available. Hiding the value in logs is a separate setting called Masked.
jenkins: What is a Jenkinsfile?
A text file in source control that defines a Jenkins Pipeline
An XML job configuration stored in JENKINS_HOME
A manifest listing the plugins Jenkins should install
A Groovy script that runs once when Jenkins starts
Storing the pipeline as a Jenkinsfile in the repository makes it versioned and reviewable along with the code (Pipeline as Code).
Which top-level block must a declarative pipeline start with?
pipeline { }
node { }
stage { }
jenkins { }
Declarative pipelines are wrapped in pipeline { }. node { } is the main block of a scripted pipeline.
Which block is the core building block of a scripted pipeline, allocating an executor and workspace?
node
pipeline
stages
agent
Scripted pipelines are Groovy code where node { } allocates an agent executor. pipeline, stages and agent belong to declarative syntax.
In a declarative pipeline, which directive specifies where the pipeline or a stage executes?
agent
node
executor
runner
agent is required at the top level (or per stage) and can be any, none, a label, or a Docker image.
What does agent none at the top level of a declarative pipeline mean?
No global agent; each stage must declare its own agent
The pipeline runs on the built-in controller node
The pipeline is disabled until an agent is assigned
Every stage runs in a default Docker container
agent none skips global allocation so stages can pick different agents, for example Linux for build and Windows for tests.
Which post condition in a declarative pipeline runs regardless of the build result?
always
success
unstable
changed
post { always { } } runs on any outcome, so it is used for cleanup and publishing reports. changed runs only when the status differs from the last run.
What is a key difference between declarative and scripted pipelines?
Declarative uses a fixed, validated structure; scripted is free-form Groovy
Scripted pipelines cannot be stored in a Jenkinsfile
Declarative pipelines cannot use any plugin steps
Scripted pipelines run only on Windows agents
Both live in a Jenkinsfile and both use plugin steps. Declarative adds a stricter syntax with validation; scripted gives full Groovy flexibility.
How do you run arbitrary Groovy logic, such as a loop, inside a declarative pipeline stage?
Wrap it in a script { } block inside steps
Wrap it in a groovy { } block inside steps
Place it in the environment { } section
Put it in options { } at the top level
The script step lets declarative pipelines run scripted Groovy. Long logic is better moved into a shared library.
Why do the Jenkins docs discourage running builds on the built-in (controller) node?
Builds there can access the controller's files and configuration
The built-in node cannot run shell steps
The built-in node supports only Java projects
Builds on it disable plugins temporarily
A build on the controller runs with access to JENKINS_HOME, including credentials and configuration. Use separate agents and set the built-in node's executors to 0.
What does the number of executors configured on a Jenkins agent control?
How many builds can run on that agent at the same time
How many stages a single pipeline may contain
How many times a failed build is retried
How many plugins the agent can load
Each executor is a slot for one build or pipeline node block, so 4 executors allow 4 concurrent builds on that agent.
What does agent { label 'linux && docker' } do?
Runs on any agent that has both the linux and docker labels
Runs on the agent named exactly 'linux && docker'
Runs on any agent that has either label
Runs in a Docker container from a linux image
Label expressions support && and ||. The build goes to an agent matching the whole expression.
Which plugin provides agent { docker { image 'node:20' } } in declarative pipelines?
Docker Pipeline
Git
Credentials Binding
Blue Ocean
The Docker Pipeline plugin adds Docker agents and docker.image() steps. Credentials Binding provides withCredentials.
You install a Jenkins plugin that depends on two other plugins. What does the plugin manager do?
Installs the required dependency plugins automatically
Refuses to install until you add them one by one
Installs it without them and disables its features
Asks you to build the dependencies from source
Jenkins resolves plugin dependencies and installs them together. Keeping plugins few and updated reduces security and compatibility issues.
What does a Multibranch Pipeline job do?
Creates a pipeline for each branch that contains a Jenkinsfile
Runs one pipeline for the default branch only
Merges all branches together before building
Requires a separate job created by hand per branch
Multibranch scans the repository and creates or removes branch jobs automatically. With supported SCM plugins it also builds pull requests.
In a multibranch pipeline, which environment variable contains the name of the branch being built?
BRANCH_NAME
GIT_BRANCH_NAME
JOB_BRANCH
CURRENT_BRANCH
Multibranch sets BRANCH_NAME for each branch job; for pull requests it is a value like PR-42.
Which declarative directive runs a stage only when building the main branch?
when { branch 'main' }
if { branch 'main' }
only { branch 'main' }
filter { branch 'main' }
when holds conditions for a stage. The branch condition works in multibranch pipelines, where the branch name is known.
How do you load a credential with id db-creds into an environment variable in a declarative pipeline?
environment { DB = credentials('db-creds') }
environment { DB = secret('db-creds') }
environment { DB = password('db-creds') }
environment { DB = vault('db-creds') }
The credentials() helper in environment binds a stored credential and masks it in the console log.
environment { DB = credentials('db-creds') } loads a username and password credential. Which extra variables appear?
DB_USR and DB_PSW
DB_USER and DB_PASS
DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD
DB_LOGIN and DB_SECRET
For username and password credentials, DB holds user:password, and DB_USR and DB_PSW hold the parts.
Which pipeline step binds credentials to variables only for the steps inside its block?
withCredentials
withSecrets
useCredentials
credentialsBlock
withCredentials (Credentials Binding plugin) exposes credentials inside a block and masks their values in the log.
Why is sh "curl -u admin:${PASS} https://api.example.com" with double quotes discouraged for secrets?
Groovy interpolates the secret into the command text, which can leak it
Double quotes stop the shell from expanding the variable
Jenkins rejects sh steps written with double quotes
The secret gets written into the Jenkinsfile in Git
With double quotes Groovy inserts the value before the shell runs, so it can appear in process listings. Single quotes let the shell expand $PASS safely.
cicd: What is the core practice of continuous integration?
Merging small changes into main often, each verified by automated build and tests
Deploying every commit to production with no human involvement
Running a full manual QA cycle before allowing any merge
Keeping feature branches separate until the release date
CI means integrating frequently into a shared mainline and checking each integration automatically. Automatic production deploys describe continuous deployment.
The CI build on main turns red. What does continuous integration practice recommend?
Fix it or revert the change right away, before new merges
Keep merging and fix it at the end of the sprint
Disable the failing tests so the build turns green
Create a new main branch from the last release
A broken mainline blocks everyone and hides new failures, so restoring it is the top priority, often by reverting quickly.
What separates continuous deployment from continuous delivery?
Every passing change goes to production with no manual release step
Code is integrated into main several times a day
Builds run on dedicated CI servers instead of laptops
Releases ship on a fixed monthly schedule
In continuous delivery every change is releasable but a person decides when to release. Continuous deployment automates that final step.
A bank's builds are always kept releasable, but a manager approves each production release. Which practice is this?
Continuous delivery
Continuous deployment
Trunk-based development
Waterfall release management
Keeping software deployable at all times with a manual approval gate is continuous delivery. Continuous deployment would release without approval.
According to the test pyramid, which kind of test should be the most numerous?
Unit tests
End-to-end UI tests
Integration tests
Manual exploratory tests
Unit tests are fast and cheap, so they form the wide base. Slower, more brittle end-to-end tests sit at the narrow top.
A test passes and fails randomly while the code stays the same. What is this called?
A flaky test
A regression test
A smoke test
A mutation test
Flaky tests erode trust in CI because failures stop meaning anything. They should be fixed or quarantined quickly.
How should a CI pipeline order its checks to give developers the fastest useful feedback?
Lint and unit tests first, slower end-to-end tests later
End-to-end tests first, unit tests at the end
All tests only after deploying to production
Random order, since order does not affect speed
Failing fast on cheap checks saves time and runner cost. Expensive suites run only after the quick ones pass.
What is a smoke test run right after a deployment?
A quick check that the most critical functions work
An exhaustive test of every feature in the system
A load test that simulates peak traffic for hours
A full penetration test of the new release
Smoke tests are fast, shallow checks (for example login and health endpoints) that decide whether deeper testing or traffic should proceed.
What is a canary deployment?
Releasing a new version to a small share of traffic first, then expanding
Running two full environments and switching all traffic at once
Updating every server at the same moment
Deploying the new version only to a staging environment
A canary exposes few users to the change while metrics are watched. Switching all traffic between two environments is blue-green.
During a canary at 5% traffic, the new version's error rate jumps well above the baseline. What should happen?
Route the traffic back to the stable version and halt the rollout
Raise the canary to 50% to collect more data
Restart the database to clear the errors
Release to all users and ship a hotfix later
The purpose of a canary is to catch problems while few users are affected. Automated rollouts often abort based on such metrics.
What is the main benefit of a canary release over releasing to everyone at once?
A faulty release affects only a small group of users
It removes the need for automated tests
It needs no extra monitoring or metrics
It makes database migrations reversible
Canaries limit the blast radius of a bad release, but they depend on good monitoring to detect problems.
How is a release performed in a blue-green deployment?
Deploy to the idle environment, then switch all traffic to it
Shift traffic gradually from 1% up to 100%
Update servers one by one in the live environment
Enable the new code with a feature flag per user
Blue runs the current version while green gets the new one. After checks pass, the router or load balancer switches traffic to green.
After a blue-green switch to green, a serious bug appears. What is the fastest rollback?
Switch traffic back to the blue environment
Rebuild the old version from source code
Restore the database from last night's backup
Redeploy the old version to the green servers
Blue still runs the previous version, so rolling back is just another traffic switch, as long as it was kept running.
Blue and green environments share one database. What does this require for schema changes?
The schema must work with both the old and new app versions
Each release must copy the full database first
Schema changes must be applied only to blue
The database must be locked during the switch
Since either version may serve traffic, migrations must be backward compatible (for example add a column before removing the old one).
Why do teams use expand-and-contract (backward-compatible) database migrations?
So the previous app version still works and can be rolled back to
So migrations finish faster on large tables
So database backups are no longer needed
So the pipeline can skip integration tests
Expanding first (adding new structures) and contracting later (removing old ones) keeps both versions working during and after a deploy.
A new feature causes errors in production and is behind a feature flag. What is the quickest mitigation?
Turn the flag off without redeploying
Revert the commit and wait for a full rebuild
Scale up the servers to absorb the errors
Delete the flag from the configuration file
Feature flags separate deployment from release, so a faulty feature can be disabled at runtime in seconds.
Why should the same build artifact be promoted from staging to production instead of being rebuilt?
It guarantees that production runs exactly what was tested
Rebuilding is not possible once tests have passed
Production servers cannot run newly built artifacts
Promoting removes the need for any rollback plan
Rebuilding can pull different dependencies or settings. Build once, deploy the same artifact everywhere.
In incident response, what does rolling forward mean?
Fixing the problem by deploying a new version that contains a fix
Redeploying the previous version to undo the change
Moving traffic to a standby region during the outage
Restoring the database to a point before the release
Rolling forward ships a fix instead of reverting. It suits small, well-understood fixes when the pipeline is fast.
What is a major benefit of defining the pipeline as code in the repository?
Pipeline changes are versioned and reviewed like application code
The pipeline no longer needs a CI server to run
Builds become faster because no YAML is parsed
Secrets can be stored safely in the same file
Pipeline as code keeps history, enables pull request review and rollback of pipeline changes. Secrets still belong in a secret store.
Which of these is one of the DORA software delivery metrics?
Change failure rate
Lines of code per developer
Story points per sprint
Percentage of code covered by tests
DORA metrics include deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and failed deployment recovery time.
kafka: What is a topic in Apache Kafka?
A named stream of records, split into one or more partitions
A single queue where each message is deleted once read
A database table with a primary key per record
A configuration profile shared by consumers
Producers write records to topics and consumers read from them. Each topic is divided into partitions that are spread across brokers.
Within which scope does Kafka guarantee the order of records?
A single partition
A whole topic
A whole broker
A whole cluster
Records are ordered by offset inside a partition. Across partitions of the same topic there is no global order.
A producer using the default partitioner sends many records with the same non-null key, and the partition count does not change. Where do they go?
All to the same partition
Round-robin across all partitions
To a random partition each time
To partition 0 regardless of the key
The default partitioner hashes the key, so equal keys map to the same partition, which keeps per-key ordering.
Can you reduce the number of partitions of an existing Kafka topic?
No, partitions can only be added, not removed
Yes, with kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions
Yes, but only while the topic is empty
Yes, after a rolling restart of the brokers
Kafka supports increasing the partition count only. To reduce it you create a new topic and migrate the data.
A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 8 active consumers. What happens?
6 consumers get one partition each and 2 stay idle
Each consumer reads three quarters of a partition
All 8 consumers read every partition
The group fails to start until 2 consumers leave
Each partition is assigned to at most one consumer in a group, so consumers beyond the partition count have nothing to read.
Two different consumer groups subscribe to the same topic. What does each group receive?
Every record of the topic, independently of the other group
Half of the records, split between the two groups
Only the records the other group skipped
Records only after the other group commits
Consumer groups are independent subscribers with their own offsets. Load is shared only among consumers inside one group.
Which event triggers a consumer group rebalance?
A consumer joining or leaving the group
A producer sending a new record
A record reaching its retention limit
A broker rolling a new log segment
Membership changes (including a consumer missing its heartbeat or poll deadline) and partition count changes cause partitions to be reassigned.
Where does a modern Kafka consumer group store its committed offsets?
In the internal __consumer_offsets topic
In ZooKeeper nodes under /consumers
In a file on the consumer's local disk
In the headers of the records it read
Modern consumers commit offsets to the compacted __consumer_offsets topic. Storing them in ZooKeeper was the old approach.
A brand-new consumer group with no committed offsets sets auto.offset.reset=earliest. Where does it start reading?
At the oldest offset still available in each partition
At the newest offset, reading only new records
At the offsets committed by other groups
It throws an error because no offset exists
earliest starts from the beginning of the retained log. The default, latest, would start at the end and read only new records.
To get at-least-once processing, when should a consumer commit offsets?
After the records have been processed
Before the records are processed
Only once when the consumer starts
Before each poll call, ahead of fetching
Committing after processing means a crash causes reprocessing, not loss. Committing first gives at-most-once delivery.
What is a Kafka broker?
A server that stores partitions and serves producers and consumers
A client library that routes records between apps
A process that only manages consumer offsets
A proxy that converts Kafka records to HTTP
A Kafka cluster consists of brokers. Each broker hosts partition replicas and handles read and write requests for them.
A topic has replication factor 3. What does that mean?
Each partition has 3 copies on different brokers
Each record is sent to 3 consumer groups
The topic is split into 3 partitions
Each record is stored 3 times on one broker
Replication factor is the number of replicas per partition. One replica is the leader, the others are followers that copy it.
Which replica of a partition handles produce requests?
The leader replica
Any in-sync follower
The cluster controller
The replica with the lowest broker id
Producers write to the partition leader, and followers replicate from it. If the leader fails, an in-sync follower is elected.
In Kafka 4.0, what manages cluster metadata now that ZooKeeper is no longer supported?
KRaft, Kafka's built-in Raft-based controller quorum
etcd, an external key-value store
Consul, through its service catalog
The first broker started in the cluster
KRaft mode replaced ZooKeeper; Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper support entirely. Controllers use the Raft protocol to store metadata in an internal log.
A producer uses acks=all. When does the leader acknowledge the write?
When all in-sync replicas have the record
As soon as the leader writes it to disk
Immediately, before writing it anywhere
When a consumer has read the record
acks=all waits for the full in-sync replica set. Combined with min.insync.replicas, it is the most durable setting.
What does enable.idempotence=true on a Kafka producer prevent?
Duplicate records in a partition caused by producer retries
Consumers processing the same record twice
Records arriving out of order across partitions
Record loss when every broker is down
The broker uses producer ids and sequence numbers to drop retried duplicates. End-to-end exactly-once also needs transactions or idempotent consumers.
How does Kafka store records inside a partition?
As an append-only log with sequential offsets
As rows that are updated in place by key
As a B-tree index sorted by timestamp
As messages removed once they are read
Each partition is a commit log: records are appended, never modified, and identified by increasing offsets. Reading does not delete them.
A topic has cleanup.policy=delete and retention.ms=604800000. What happens to its data?
Log segments older than 7 days become eligible for deletion
Records are deleted once every group has read them
The whole topic is deleted after 7 days
Only the latest record per key is kept
604800000 ms is 7 days. Deletion works on closed segments, so some records may live slightly longer than the limit.
A topic uses cleanup.policy=compact. What does Kafka guarantee to keep?
At least the latest record for each key
Only the newest 1000 records
Only the first record for each key
Only records that have a null key
Compaction removes older records with the same key, keeping the newest value. It suits changelogs and state such as user profiles.
A consumer must process records of one customer in order while scaling to many consumers. What should the producer do?
Use the customer id as the record key
Send every record without a key
Create one topic per consumer instance
Set the partition count to 1
Keyed records for one customer land in one partition, which one consumer reads in order, while other customers spread across partitions.
rabbitmq: How does a direct exchange route a message?
To queues whose binding key exactly matches the routing key
To every queue bound to the exchange, ignoring the key
To queues whose binding pattern matches with wildcards
To queues whose binding headers match the message headers
Direct exchanges use exact matching. Copying to all bound queues is fanout, wildcards are topic exchanges, headers matching is a headers exchange.
Which exchange type ignores the routing key and copies each message to all bound queues?
fanout
direct
topic
headers
A fanout exchange broadcasts every message to all queues bound to it, which fits pub/sub notifications.
A queue is bound to a topic exchange with binding key logs.*. Which routing key reaches it?
logs.error
logs.error.db
logs
error.logs
In topic bindings * matches exactly one dot-separated word, so logs.error matches but logs and logs.error.db do not.
A queue is bound to a topic exchange with binding key #.error. Which routing key reaches it?
app.db.error
app.error.db
app.db.errors
errors
# matches zero or more words, so any key whose last word is error matches. errors is a different word.
How does a headers exchange decide where to route a message?
It matches message header values against binding arguments
It matches the routing key against a regular expression
It sends the message to the queue named in a header
It hashes the headers to pick one queue
Headers exchanges ignore the routing key. The x-match argument (all or any) sets whether every or just one header must match.
A message is published to the default exchange (empty name) with routing key tasks. Where does it go?
To the queue named tasks
To every queue on the virtual host
To a new queue created automatically
Nowhere, the default exchange drops it
Every queue is automatically bound to the default exchange with its own name as the binding key.
What is needed for messages to survive a RabbitMQ broker restart?
A durable queue and messages published as persistent
A durable exchange, with transient messages
An exclusive queue and persistent messages
An auto-delete queue and persistent messages
A non-durable queue disappears on restart, and transient messages are not kept even in a durable queue. Both are needed.
What characterizes an exclusive queue in RabbitMQ?
Used by one connection only, deleted when it closes
It accepts messages from one exchange only
It delivers each message to one consumer only
It survives restarts but cannot be shared
Exclusive queues are tied to one connection, which suits temporary reply queues. Delivering each message to one consumer is normal queue behavior.
In RabbitMQ 3.8 and later, which queue type is recommended for replicated, highly available data?
Quorum queues
Classic mirrored queues
Exclusive queues
Auto-delete queues
Quorum queues replicate data with the Raft protocol. Classic queue mirroring was deprecated and removed in RabbitMQ 4.0.
What is a binding in RabbitMQ?
A rule linking an exchange to a queue, optionally by key
A TCP connection between a client and the broker
An acknowledgment sent by a consumer
A setting that limits the length of a queue
Bindings tell an exchange which queues should receive which messages. Without a matching binding, the exchange has nowhere to route.
A message is published to a direct exchange with a routing key that matches no binding, and mandatory is false. What happens?
The message is silently discarded
It waits in the exchange until a binding appears
It is returned to the publisher with an error
It is sent to the default queue of the vhost
Exchanges do not store messages. With mandatory set, an unroutable message is returned to the publisher instead (unless an alternate exchange is configured).
A consumer using manual acknowledgments crashes before acking a message. What happens to that message?
It is requeued and delivered again
It is lost because it was already delivered
It goes straight to the dead-letter exchange
It stays locked to that consumer forever
When the channel or connection closes, unacknowledged messages return to the queue and are redelivered with the redelivered flag set.
A consumer rejects a message with basic.nack and requeue=false. The queue has a dead-letter exchange configured. What happens?
The message is republished to the dead-letter exchange
The message goes back to the head of the queue
The message is dropped and the DLX is ignored
The publisher receives the message back
Rejections without requeue are one of the dead-letter triggers, along with TTL expiry and queue length limits.
What does basic.qos with prefetch_count=10 do for a consumer?
Caps unacked messages in flight on that channel at 10
Delivers messages in batches of exactly 10
Limits the queue to 10 stored messages
Retries each failed message up to 10 times
Prefetch caps in-flight unacked messages so work is spread fairly among consumers and a slow consumer is not flooded.
What is the main risk of consuming with automatic acknowledgment (autoAck) enabled?
A crash during processing loses the message
Each message is delivered to every consumer
Messages are redelivered in an endless loop
Messages pile up because acks do not arrive
With autoAck the broker considers a message done as soon as it is sent, so a crash mid-processing loses it.
RabbitMQ's model of exchanges, queues and bindings comes from which protocol?
AMQP 0-9-1
MQTT 3.1.1
STOMP 1.2
HTTP/2
AMQP 0-9-1 defines exchanges, queues and bindings and is RabbitMQ's core protocol. MQTT and STOMP are supported through plugins.
In AMQP 0-9-1, what is a channel?
A virtual connection multiplexed over one TCP connection
A separate TCP connection opened per message
A named queue shared by several consumers
A routing rule stored on an exchange
Applications open one connection and many channels over it, avoiding the cost of many TCP connections.
Which port does RabbitMQ use by default for AMQP 0-9-1 connections without TLS?
5672 is the AMQP port. 15672 is the management UI, 1883 is MQTT and 4222 is NATS.
Which of these causes a message to be dead-lettered?
Its TTL expires while it waits in the queue
A consumer acknowledges it successfully
It is published to a fanout exchange
The consumer reaches its prefetch limit
Messages are dead-lettered when rejected without requeue, when their TTL expires, or when a queue length limit drops them.
How do you attach a dead-letter exchange to a queue?
Set the x-dead-letter-exchange argument or a policy
Bind the queue to an exchange named dlx
Publish messages with delivery_mode set to 3
Enable a dead-letter flag on each consumer
The DLX is configured per queue, ideally with a policy so it can be changed without redeclaring the queue.
nats: What delivery guarantee does core NATS (without JetStream) provide?
At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
Persistent ordered delivery
Core NATS is fire-and-forget: messages are kept only in memory and delivered to currently connected subscribers. JetStream adds persistence.
In core NATS, a message is published to a subject that has no subscribers. What happens?
The message is discarded
The server stores it until a subscriber arrives
The publisher receives an error for every publish
It is sent to a default dead-letter subject
Core NATS has no storage, so messages with no interested subscribers are dropped. Use JetStream if messages must be kept.
Three subscribers join the same queue group on subject orders. One message is published. Who receives it?
One member of the queue group
All three subscribers
The first subscriber that joined
None, queue groups need JetStream
Queue groups load-balance: each message goes to one randomly chosen member, which lets services scale horizontally.
Two subscribers on subject alerts use no queue group. One message is published. Who receives it?
Both subscribers
Only one, chosen at random
Only the oldest subscription
Neither, until one acks it
Plain subscriptions are fan-out: every matching subscriber gets a copy.
Which subject matches the subscription orders.*?
orders.new
orders.new.eu
orders
new.orders
* matches exactly one token. orders.new.eu has two tokens after orders, and orders has none.
Which subject matches the subscription orders.>?
orders.eu.new
orders
order.eu
eu.orders.new
> matches one or more trailing tokens, so it needs at least one token after orders.
Which character separates tokens in a NATS subject such as orders.eu.new?
A dot
A slash
A colon
A hyphen
Subjects are dot-separated token hierarchies, and wildcards match whole tokens.
Where can the > wildcard appear in a NATS subscription subject?
Only as the last token
Only as the first token
At any position, any number of times
Only in subjects used for publishing
> is the full wildcard and must be the final token, for example events.>. Publishers cannot use wildcards.
How does the request-reply pattern work in NATS?
The request carries a unique inbox subject, and the responder publishes the reply to it
The server opens a direct TCP connection between both clients
The responder writes the reply into a JetStream stream
The requester polls the responder's subject until a reply
Request-reply is built on pub/sub: the client subscribes to a unique inbox, sends the request with that reply subject, and waits.
On NATS server 2.2 or later, a client sends a request to a subject that has no subscribers. What does it get?
An immediate no responders error
A reply with an empty body
Nothing until its timeout expires
A reply from the server's system account
Since 2.2, servers send a no responders status to clients that support headers, so the requester fails fast instead of waiting.
In a NATS cluster, a client on server A publishes, and a matching subscriber is connected to server B. What happens?
Server A forwards the message to B through their route connection
Nothing, clients must connect to the same server
The subscriber must also connect to server A
The message is copied to every server's disk first
Cluster servers share subscription interest over routes, so messages reach subscribers on any server.
What is a stream in NATS JetStream?
Storage that captures messages published to a set of subjects
A single consumer's position in a subject
A TCP connection between two clusters
A temporary inbox for request replies
Streams persist messages from their configured subjects, with limits on age, size or count. Consumers read from streams.
What is a JetStream consumer?
A stateful view on a stream that tracks delivered and acked messages
A client subscription to a core NATS subject
A copy of a stream kept in another cluster
A process that deletes expired stream messages
Consumers keep delivery state on the server, enabling acknowledgments, redelivery and resuming from where a client left off.
According to the NATS docs, which JetStream consumer type is recommended for new projects, especially for scaling workers?
Pull consumers
Push consumers
Ordered push consumers
Ephemeral push consumers
Pull consumers let each client fetch batches at its own pace, which scales horizontally and gives natural flow control.
A JetStream stream uses the WorkQueue retention policy. What happens after a message is acknowledged?
It is removed from the stream
It stays until the stream's age limit
It is copied to every other consumer
It is moved to a dead-letter stream
WorkQueue retention deletes a message once it is consumed and acked, so each message is processed once.
What is the difference between a durable and an ephemeral JetStream consumer?
A durable consumer keeps its state after clients disconnect
A durable consumer stores messages on disk, not in memory
An ephemeral consumer can only read the last message
An ephemeral consumer acknowledges messages automatically
Durable consumers have a name and persist their progress. Ephemeral consumers are cleaned up after a period of inactivity.
A JetStream consumer uses explicit acks. A message is not acked within the AckWait time. What happens?
The message is redelivered
The message is deleted from the stream
The consumer is removed by the server
The stream stops accepting new messages
Unacked messages are redelivered after AckWait, up to MaxDeliver attempts, giving at-least-once delivery.
What is the Nats-Msg-Id header used for when publishing to JetStream?
Dropping duplicate publishes within the stream's duplicate window
Choosing which consumer receives the message
Setting the order of messages in the stream
Routing the message to a specific server
If the same Nats-Msg-Id arrives again within the duplicate window, JetStream ignores it, which makes publisher retries safe.
How do NATS servers form a cluster?
They connect to each other with route connections in a full mesh
They register in a central ZooKeeper ensemble
They share state through one common database
They elect one server that relays all messages
Each server connects to every other server via routes, and the cluster gossips topology to clients so they can fail over.
Why is a replica count of 3 common for JetStream streams in a cluster?
Raft needs a majority, so 3 replicas tolerate one failed server
JetStream accepts only odd stream names
3 replicas triple the publish throughput
Clients can connect to at most 3 servers
Replicated streams use Raft. With 3 replicas, 2 still form a majority when one server is down; 2 replicas would tolerate none.
airflow: An Airflow DAG sets dependencies a >> b >> c >> a. What happens?
Airflow rejects the DAG because it contains a cycle
The tasks loop forever in that order
Airflow runs each task exactly twice
Airflow ignores the last dependency
DAG means directed acyclic graph. A cycle makes the DAG invalid, and it fails to import with an error.
What does extract >> transform mean in an Airflow DAG?
transform runs after extract (it is downstream)
extract runs after transform
Both tasks run at the same time
transform gets extract's code
>> sets the right side as downstream. It is equivalent to extract.set_downstream(transform).
A DAG has [a, b] >> c and default settings. When does c run?
After both a and b succeed
After either a or b succeeds
At the same time as a and b
Before a and b
The default trigger rule is all_success, so c waits for every upstream task to succeed.
A cleanup task must run after its upstream tasks finish, whether they succeeded or failed. Which trigger_rule fits?
all_done
all_success
one_success
none_failed
all_done runs once all upstream tasks are finished in any state. none_failed would skip it if an upstream task failed.
What is the relationship between an operator and a task in Airflow?
A task is an instance of an operator inside a DAG
An operator is a group of tasks that run together
A task is a Python package that contains operators
Operators and tasks are unrelated concepts
Operators are templates such as BashOperator. Instantiating one with a task_id in a DAG creates a task.
What is a sensor in Airflow?
An operator that waits for a condition, such as a file appearing
A plugin that monitors the scheduler's memory usage
A task that sends alerts when other tasks fail
A metric exporter for the Airflow web UI
Sensors poke a condition repeatedly and succeed once it is true, letting downstream tasks start.
Why set mode='reschedule' on a sensor that may wait for hours?
It frees the worker slot between checks instead of sleeping
It checks the condition more often than poke mode
It retries the upstream task that failed
It makes the sensor run on the scheduler
In poke mode the sensor holds a worker slot the whole time. Reschedule mode releases it and is rescheduled for the next check.
A deferrable operator defers while waiting for an external job. Which Airflow component does the waiting?
The triggerer, using asynchronous triggers
The scheduler, in its main loop
The webserver, through a background thread
The same worker, sleeping in a loop
Deferred tasks release their worker. The triggerer runs many async triggers efficiently and resumes the task when one fires.
In the TaskFlow API, a @task function returns a small dictionary. What happens to it?
It is pushed to XCom automatically
It is discarded after the task ends
It is written to an Airflow Variable
It is printed but cannot be used
TaskFlow stores return values as XCom (key return_value) and passes them to downstream tasks that take them as arguments.
Why should you avoid passing a large DataFrame through XCom with the default backend?
XComs live in the metadata database and suit small data
XComs are deleted before the next task starts
XComs can only hold integer values
XComs are visible only to the scheduler
Large objects bloat the metadata DB and slow Airflow. Store data in object storage and pass a path, or use a custom XCom backend.
What does ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='extract') return inside a later task?
The value task extract returned (key return_value)
The log output written by task extract
The final state recorded for task extract
The rendered template of task extract
Without a key argument, xcom_pull reads the return_value XCom of the given task.
A daily DAG has a start_date 30 days ago and catchup=True. What happens when it is first unpaused?
The scheduler creates runs for each missed interval
Only one run for the current day is created
Nothing until the next scheduled time
All missed runs merge into one big run
With catchup enabled, Airflow backfills every interval between start_date and now. Set catchup=False to run only the latest one.
What does the cron expression 0 6 * * 1 mean as an Airflow schedule?
06:00 every Monday
06:00 on the 1st of each month
Every 6 hours on Mondays
01:00 on every 6th day
Fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. Day of week 1 is Monday.
In Airflow 2.x, a @daily DAG run has the data interval Jan 1 00:00 to Jan 2 00:00. When does it start?
Shortly after Jan 2 00:00, when the interval ends
At Jan 1 00:00, when the interval begins
At noon on Jan 1, midway through it
At Jan 3 00:00, one day after it ends
With the default timetable in Airflow 2.x, a run processes a finished interval, so it starts after the interval closes.
Which executor runs tasks in parallel as processes on the scheduler's machine, fitting a single-node setup?
LocalExecutor
CeleryExecutor
KubernetesExecutor
SequentialExecutor
LocalExecutor spawns local processes. Celery and Kubernetes executors distribute work across machines, and SequentialExecutor runs one task at a time.
Which Airflow executor launches a new pod for each task?
KubernetesExecutor
CeleryExecutor
LocalExecutor
DebugExecutor
KubernetesExecutor creates a pod per task instance, giving isolation and per-task resources.
Which extra component does the CeleryExecutor need?
A message broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ
A Kubernetes cluster for task pods
A Spark cluster to run operators
A second metadata database replica
The scheduler sends tasks through the broker to Celery workers, which may run on many machines.
Where should a task get its database credentials from in Airflow?
An Airflow Connection referenced by its conn_id
Constants hard-coded in the DAG file
An XCom pushed by an earlier task
A comment at the top of the DAG file
Connections store hosts and credentials centrally (optionally in a secrets backend), and hooks or operators look them up by conn_id.
Why should you avoid calling Variable.get() at the top level of a DAG file?
Each frequent DAG file parse would query the database
Variables cannot be read outside an operator
Top-level calls run only once a year
It makes the Variable read-only afterwards
Top-level code runs on every parse. Read Variables inside tasks or through Jinja templates such as {{ var.value.name }}.
Which environment variable defines an Airflow connection with conn_id my_db?
AIRFLOW_CONN_MY_DB
AIRFLOW_CONNECTION_MY_DB
AIRFLOW__CONN__MY_DB
CONN_MY_DB
Variables named AIRFLOW_CONN_<CONN_ID> in upper case define connections, as a URI or JSON. Double underscores are for config options.
dbt: What is a dbt model?
A SQL SELECT in a .sql file, built as a table or view
A YAML file that lists the columns of a source table
A Python class that maps tables to objects
A stored procedure that dbt calls on a schedule
Models are SQL SELECT queries; dbt wraps them in the DDL needed to create the relation in the warehouse.
Which materialization does dbt use for a model when none is configured?
view
table
incremental
ephemeral
The default materialization is view. You can change it per model or per folder in dbt_project.yml.
A model starts with {{ config(materialized='table') }}. What does dbt run do with it?
Rebuilds it as a physical table on each run
Creates a view that refreshes automatically
Appends only new rows to the existing table
Inlines it as a CTE into dependent models
Table materialization recreates the table from the query each run. Appending new rows is incremental, and inlining is ephemeral.
What happens to a model with materialized='ephemeral'?
Not built in the warehouse; inlined as a CTE where used
It is created as a temporary table that lasts one day
It is built only when you run dbt run --ephemeral
It is created as a view and dropped after tests pass
Ephemeral models exist only as reusable SQL. Models that ref them get the code inserted as a common table expression.
Why write {{ ref('stg_orders') }} instead of hard-coding analytics.stg_orders?
dbt resolves the right relation per environment and records the dependency
It runs stg_orders again before every query that uses it
It copies the data of stg_orders into the new model
It makes the query faster by caching stg_orders
ref picks the schema for the current target (dev or prod) and builds the DAG so models run in dependency order.
What does dbt run --select stg_orders+ build?
stg_orders and every model downstream of it
stg_orders and every model upstream of it
Only models whose names start with stg_orders
stg_orders and its tests, but no other models
A + after the name adds descendants; a + before it (+stg_orders) adds ancestors.
A source named shop with a table orders is declared in YAML. How do you select from it in a model?
{{ source('shop', 'orders') }}
{{ ref('shop.orders') }}
{{ source('orders') }}
{{ raw('shop', 'orders') }}
source() takes the source name and table name, resolves the database and schema from YAML, and adds the source to the lineage graph.
What does dbt source freshness check?
How recently source data loaded, against warn and error limits
Whether each source table has a primary key column
Whether the source schema matches the YAML columns
How long each model took to build last time
It reads the max loaded_at_field value and warns or errors if the data is older than the configured thresholds.
Which are dbt's four built-in generic data tests?
unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships
unique, not_null, primary_key and foreign_key
not_null, positive, in_range and is_date
unique, required, enum and lookup
These four ship with dbt. Packages such as dbt_utils add more, and you can write your own generic tests.
You write a singular test as a SQL file in the tests/ folder. When does it fail?
When the query returns one or more rows
When the query returns zero rows
When the query takes over a minute
When the query uses a ref() call
dbt tests select the failing records, so any returned row counts as a failure.
A relationships test is defined on orders.customer_id pointing to customers.id. What does it check?
Every customer_id in orders exists in customers.id
Every customers.id has at least one order
customer_id values in orders are unique
orders and customers have the same row count
It enforces referential integrity from child to parent. Null customer_id values are not counted as failures.
Which command generates dbt's documentation site files?
dbt docs generate
dbt docs build
dbt generate docs
dbt build --docs
dbt docs generate compiles the project and writes catalog and manifest files. dbt docs serve then hosts the site locally.
Where do you write a column description so that it appears in dbt docs?
Under the model's columns in a YAML properties file
In a comment on the first line of the model SQL
In the dbt_project.yml vars block
In a README.md inside the models folder
Descriptions go in the description field of a model or column in YAML, and can use doc blocks for longer text.
In an incremental model, when does the SQL inside {% if is_incremental() %} apply?
When the table exists and it is not a full refresh
Only on the very first run of the model
Only when run with the --full-refresh flag
On every run, whatever the table state
is_incremental() is true for incremental models whose table already exists, unless --full-refresh is used. It typically filters to new rows.
Inside an incremental model, what does {{ this }} refer to?
The model's own existing table in the warehouse
The model that runs right before it
The source declared first in YAML
The temporary table of new rows
{{ this }} lets you query the current target, for example where updated_at > (select max(updated_at) from {{ this }}).
What does setting unique_key on an incremental model do?
Updates rows matching the key instead of only appending
Adds a unique constraint to the warehouse table
Removes duplicate rows from the source data
Makes dbt run the model only once per key
With unique_key, strategies such as merge or delete+insert replace matching rows; without it, new rows are only appended.
What does dbt run --full-refresh do to an incremental model?
Rebuilds the whole table from scratch
Processes only rows added since the last run
Refreshes the view on top of the table
Deletes the model without rebuilding it
--full-refresh drops and recreates the incremental table, needed after logic or schema changes.
What problem do dbt snapshots solve?
Recording how mutable source rows change over time (SCD Type 2)
Backing up the whole warehouse before each run
Caching query results to speed up dashboards
Freezing a model so it stops being rebuilt
Snapshots keep historical versions of rows that are overwritten in the source, so you can see past states.
Which columns does dbt add to a snapshot table to mark when each row version was valid?
dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to
valid_start and valid_end
dbt_created_at and dbt_deleted_at
snapshot_from and snapshot_to
A current row has a null dbt_valid_to (by default). When a change is detected, the old row is closed and a new one inserted.
A source table has no reliable updated_at column. Which snapshot strategy should you use?
check, comparing the listed check_cols
timestamp, using the load date
incremental, with a unique_key
append, keeping every new row
The timestamp strategy needs a trustworthy updated_at. The check strategy compares column values to detect changes.
prometheus: Which Prometheus metric type fits the total number of HTTP requests served?
Counter
Gauge
Histogram
Summary
A counter only increases (resetting on restart), which suits cumulative totals. You then use rate() to get requests per second.
Which metric type fits current memory usage, which goes up and down?
Gauge
Counter
Histogram
Summary
Gauges represent values that can increase and decrease, such as memory, temperature or queue length.
What is the main advantage of a Histogram over a Summary in Prometheus?
Its buckets can be aggregated across instances to compute quantiles
It computes exact quantiles inside the client
It uses fewer time series per metric
It needs no bucket configuration at all
Summary quantiles are computed per instance and cannot be meaningfully averaged. Histogram buckets can be summed, then passed to histogram_quantile.
A classic histogram http_request_duration_seconds is exposed. Which series does it produce?
_bucket, _sum and _count
_min, _max and _avg
_total, _rate and _last
Each bucket series carries an le label with its upper bound, plus a total sum and a count of observations.
What does rate(http_requests_total[5m]) return?
The per-second average increase over the last 5 minutes
The total number of requests in the last 5 minutes
The highest value seen in the last 5 minutes
The number of samples scraped in 5 minutes
rate() calculates the per-second rate of a counter over the range and handles counter resets. increase() gives the total increase instead.
You want to see how much a gauge temperature_celsius changed over the last hour. Which function fits?
delta(temperature_celsius[1h])
rate(temperature_celsius[1h])
increase(temperature_celsius[1h])
irate(temperature_celsius[1h])
delta() is meant for gauges. rate, increase and irate assume counters and treat any drop as a counter reset.
What does sum by (status) (rate(http_requests_total[5m])) show?
The request rate per status code, summed over all instances
The request rate per instance, ignoring status codes
The total requests ever served per status code
One number for all requests and all statuses
by (status) keeps only the status label and sums away the others, such as instance and job.
Why must le stay in the by clause of histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(x_bucket[5m])))?
histogram_quantile needs the bucket boundaries stored in le
le holds the instance name used for grouping
le sets the 5 minute window of the query
Without le the query returns the average
Dropping le would merge all buckets into one series, leaving histogram_quantile nothing to interpolate between.
What does the selector up[5m] return?
A range vector with each series' samples from the last 5 minutes
An instant vector with the latest value of each series
A single number averaged over 5 minutes
The series that were up for all 5 minutes
Adding [5m] turns a selector into a range vector, which functions such as rate() and avg_over_time() take as input.
What does up == 0 for a target indicate?
The last scrape of that target failed
The target reported zero requests
The target was just added to config
The target exposes no metrics yet
Prometheus writes the synthetic up metric for each scrape: 1 when it succeeded, 0 when it failed.
How does Prometheus normally collect metrics from applications?
It pulls them by scraping HTTP endpoints such as /metrics
Applications push them to Prometheus over gRPC
It reads them from the application's log files
It queries a SQL table that applications write to
Prometheus uses a pull model with configured or discovered targets. Pushing is limited to special cases through the Pushgateway.
A short-lived batch job finishes before Prometheus can scrape it. What is the usual solution?
Push its metrics to a Pushgateway that Prometheus scrapes
Increase scrape_interval to 1 second
Write the metrics to a log file
Add the job as a recording rule
The Pushgateway holds metrics from service-level batch jobs so Prometheus can scrape them later.
Which prometheus.yml setting controls how often targets are scraped?
scrape_interval
evaluation_interval
scrape_timeout
poll_interval
scrape_interval sets scrape frequency, globally or per job. evaluation_interval controls how often rules are evaluated.
In Kubernetes, how does Prometheus find pods to scrape without static IP addresses?
With kubernetes_sd_configs service discovery
With static_configs listing every pod IP
By scanning the cluster network for open ports
By reading pod logs for a metrics address
Kubernetes service discovery watches the API server for pods, services and endpoints, and relabeling selects which ones to scrape.
Which configuration drops or rewrites targets based on discovered labels before they are scraped?
relabel_configs
metric_relabel_configs
alert_relabel_configs
write_relabel_configs
relabel_configs works on targets before the scrape. metric_relabel_configs works on scraped samples, after the scrape.
Prometheus evaluates alerting rules. What does Alertmanager do with the resulting alerts?
Groups, deduplicates and routes them to receivers such as email or Slack
Evaluates PromQL expressions to decide which alerts fire
Scrapes targets again to confirm each alert
Stores the alerts as new time series for graphs
Alertmanager handles notification: grouping, deduplication, routing, silences and inhibition. Rule evaluation stays in Prometheus.
An alerting rule has for: 10m. What does that do?
The condition must stay true for 10 minutes before the alert fires
The alert repeats its notification every 10 minutes
The alert resolves on its own after 10 minutes
The rule is evaluated once every 10 minutes
Until the duration passes, the alert is in the pending state. This avoids alerts for brief spikes.
You plan one hour of maintenance on a database and want to mute its alerts. What do you create in Alertmanager?
A silence matching the database's alerts
A new alerting rule with for: 1h
A receiver with no integrations
A recording rule that hides the alerts
Silences mute matching alerts for a set time window and expire on their own, without changing any configuration.
Why use Prometheus recording rules?
To precompute expensive queries into new series for faster dashboards and alerts
To record raw scrape responses for later debugging
To send alerts to receivers through Alertmanager
To store metrics in a remote long-term database
Recording rules evaluate an expression periodically and save the result as a new time series, so queries read it cheaply.
Which name follows the Prometheus naming convention for a recording rule?
job:http_requests:rate5m
rate5m_http_requests_by_job
http.requests.rate.5m
record_http_requests_job_5m
The recommended form is level:metric:operations, where level shows the aggregation labels kept, here job.
grafana: Grafana shows a dashboard of metrics collected by Prometheus. Where is the metric data stored?
In Prometheus; Grafana queries it when the dashboard loads
In Grafana's own built-in time series store
In the browser's local storage after import
In the JSON model of the dashboard
Grafana is a visualization layer that queries data sources on demand. Its own database stores dashboards, users and settings.
Which query language do you write in a panel that uses a Prometheus data source?
PromQL
LogQL
SQL
TraceQL
Each data source has its own query editor and language. LogQL is for Loki and TraceQL for Tempo.
Which Grafana project is a log aggregation system that you add as a data source?
Loki
Tempo
Mimir
Pyroscope
Loki stores logs, Tempo stores traces, Mimir stores metrics and Pyroscope stores continuous profiles.
How is a Grafana dashboard represented for export, import and version control?
As a JSON model
As a YAML Helm chart
As a SQL dump
As a PNG with metadata
Every dashboard has a JSON model that you can view in settings, export and keep in Git.
How can Grafana load data sources and dashboards from files automatically at startup?
With provisioning YAML files in the provisioning directory
By placing JSON files in the browser's downloads
By running the grafana-cli import-all command
By adding them to the panel's query options
Provisioning lets you manage data sources, dashboards and alerting as code, which suits automated deployments.
What is a row used for in a Grafana dashboard?
Grouping related panels into a section that can collapse
Adding one more query to a table panel
Filtering every panel to one time range
Linking two dashboards together
Rows organize large dashboards. Collapsed rows also skip loading their panels until they are expanded.
A panel shows raw byte counts like 1500000. How do you make Grafana display readable sizes such as MB?
Set the panel's Unit standard option to a bytes unit
Divide the value by 1000000 in a value mapping
Change the data source type to a storage source
Switch the panel from Time series to Table
Units in Standard options format values automatically, scaling bytes to KB, MB and GB.
What do thresholds in a Grafana panel do?
Change colors when a value crosses defined levels
Drop data points above a defined level
Send an alert when a value crosses a level
Limit how many series the panel displays
Thresholds color values, backgrounds or lines (for example green, orange, red). Alerting is configured separately in alert rules.
You want to join the results of two queries into one table before display. Which panel feature does that?
Transformations
Overrides
Thresholds
Value mappings
Transformations reshape query results, for example joining by field, filtering or calculating new fields, before visualization.
In a time series panel, how do you give only one specific series a different color and axis?
Add a field override that matches that series
Edit the data source to rename the series
Create a new threshold for that series
Add a dashboard variable for that series
Overrides apply settings to selected fields or series, while standard options apply to all of them.
A panel shows 1 or 0 for service health. How do you display UP and DOWN instead?
Add value mappings from 1 to UP and from 0 to DOWN
Add transformations that rename the field
Add thresholds at 0 and 1 with labels
Set the panel unit to a boolean type
Value mappings translate raw values or ranges into text and colors, useful for status panels.
A dashboard variable named instance uses the query label_values(up, instance). What does it do?
Fills a dropdown with the instance label values from Prometheus
Creates one dashboard per instance automatically
Filters every panel to instances that are up
Counts how many instances are currently up
Query variables load their options from the data source; label_values returns the values of a label on the given metric.
